q: Your Delta has skated across the bottom twice. The charter base offers a spare anchor. Which type do you take?
a: A fisherman (Admiralty) anchor
o: A Danforth-type flat anchor
A Bruce claw anchor
A mushroom anchor
why: A fisherman's narrow fluke pierces weed and hooks rock where broad flukes skate.

fig.title: Pilot notes for the bay
lines: Spare anchors held at the base

q: Your only anchor is well set in sand. What is the main concern tonight?
a: It may break out and not reset when the pull reverses
o: It will dig in too deep to raise in the morning
It holds well only in mud, not in sand
It needs at least 10:1 scope to hold at all
why: Danforth types hold hard in sand and mud but often pull out and clog when the wind swings round.

q: You plan to anchor on the shallow patch off Kalamos shown on the chart. What does the abbreviation tell you?
a: Weed — the anchor may skate; look for sand
o: Wreck debris — an obstruction to avoid
Wide shelf — plenty of room to swing
Weak current — no stream to allow for
why: Wd = weed on the chart; anchors often fail to dig through it.

q: You want a second anchor for kedging: light, stowing flat in a cockpit locker, holding well in sand and mud. Which type?
a: A Danforth type
o: A Bruce claw
A fisherman with a stock
A folding grapnel
why: Danforth types give high holding for their weight in sand and mud and stow flat.

q: You take the dinghy to snorkel off a rocky point near Paxos and want to anchor it. What do you use?
a: A small folding grapnel on a light line
o: The yacht's spare Delta and its chain
A small Danforth that needs sand to bite
The heavy fisherman from the yacht
why: A light grapnel hooks into rock and is easy to handle from a dinghy.

q: Looking down through clear water you see this bottom. Where do you drop the anchor?
a: B — on the sand, clear of the seagrass
o: A — the seagrass will grip the anchor
A — the meadow cushions anchor and chain
Between them, with the chain on the grass
why: Posidonia seagrass is protected and holds poorly; anchor and chain belong on sand.

fig.note: Seen from the bow, depth about 6 m

q: You are backing down on the anchor. What is happening and what do you do?
a: It is skating — lift it and try another spot
o: It is setting well — add more revs
The chain is settling — wait ten minutes
It has hooked a rock — ease off and stay
why: A juddering chain and moving transits mean the anchor is not biting.

q: You dragged in the night and have lifted the anchor. You see this. What do you do before trying again?
a: Clear it and drop on a patch of clean sand
o: Drop again in the same spot with more chain
Leave it on — it adds weight to the anchor
Fit the heavier spare and drop here again
why: A clump of weed on the tip stops any anchor digging in; change the spot too.

fig.title: Anchor at the bow roller
lines: A ball of weed jammed on the tip
Clean sand patches near the beach

q: The best sandy patch in the bay is crossed by the line shown on your chart. What do you do?
a: Anchor well clear — it marks a submarine cable
o: Anchor on it — it marks a sand bar
Anchor on it — it is a depth contour
Anchor beside it — it marks the swimming zone
why: A magenta wavy line is a submarine cable; never anchor on or near it.

fig.title: Chart extract
lines: Magenta wavy line, beach to open sea
Sand, 5 m, either side of it
Rock along the rest of the shore

q: You are about to anchor for a gusty night. How much chain do you pay out?
why: (6 m depth + 1 m bow height) × 5 = 35 m; measure from the roller, not the surface.

q: You are laying the kedge as your main anchor. How much rode do you pay out in total?
why: (8 m + 1 m bow height) × 7 = 63 m; chain-and-rope needs about 6–8:1.

q: You anchor at low water in a bay near Trieste. What length of chain do you let out?
why: Use the depth at high water plus bow height: (5 + 1 + 1) × 4 = 28 m.

q: You check the chain counter after anchoring. Is it enough for tonight, and what do you do?
a: About 4:1 — let out more if there is room
o: About 5:1 — that is enough for F6
About 7:1 — shorten so you swing less
About 3:1 — lift and re-anchor at once
why: 30 m ÷ (6 + 1 m) ≈ 4.3:1; aim for 5–7:1 when strong wind is forecast.

q: Your crew wants to leave the chain like this so the boat swings less. What is the risk?
a: The chain lifts the shank and pulls the anchor out
o: None — a tight chain holds the boat better
None — the anchor's weight holds the boat
The anchor digs in too deep to raise
why: An anchor holds only when the pull along the bottom is near horizontal.

q: What is the deepest water you can anchor in tonight?
a: 9 m
o: 7 m
why: 50 m ÷ 5 = 10 m from roller to seabed, less 1 m bow height = 9 m of water.

q: You anchor in this spot. Will you stay afloat at low water?
a: Yes — about 0.4 m under the keel
o: No — you will touch at low water
Yes — about 1.1 m under the keel
Yes — about 0.7 m under the keel
why: 3 − 0.7 = 2.3 m at low water; 2.3 − 1.9 m draught = 0.4 m clearance.

q: Your crew wants to save weight by shackling the nylon kedge rope straight onto the anchor. What is wrong with that?
a: The rope chafes on the bottom and lifts the shank
o: Nothing — rope alone holds just as well
The rope sinks and fouls the flukes
Rope stretches too little to absorb gusts
why: A few metres of chain at the anchor keeps the pull low and resists chafe.

q: Which spot gives you the quietest night?
a: A — tucked in behind the headland
o: B — in the middle, with the most room
C — close under the beach at the head
Any of them — the wind is only light
why: Swell, not just wind, decides comfort; anchor behind land that blocks it.

fig.note: Wind NW F3 · old swell rolling in from the SW

q: You are anchored here for the night. What do you do?
a: Leave before dark for a bay sheltered from the west
o: Stay, and let out more chain before midnight
Stay with the anchor alarm on and sleep
Move closer in, towards the beach
why: A bay open to the forecast wind becomes a lee shore; move while it is light.

fig.note: Forecast: wind W F6 after midnight

q: Before dark, what do you prepare in case you must leave in the night?
a: An exit track on the plotter, hazards marked
o: A plan to wait for daylight, whatever happens
The anchor alarm set to its widest radius
The dinghy in the water, ready to tow you out
why: Plan the night exit in daylight, when you can still see the rocks.

fig.title: Unfamiliar bay, Ionian
lines: Rocks either side of the entrance
Wind may shift in the night

q: You arrive in this bay. Where do you let go your anchor?
a: C — well to one side, clear of its swing
o: A — ahead of it, in the open water
B — close astern, in its lee
Close alongside it, on short scope
why: Never drop over another boat's chain; keep both swinging circles apart.

labels: yacht at anchor, 40 m chain out

q: You want to anchor in the remaining gap for the night. How do you do it?
a: Take a shore line too, like your neighbours
o: Swing free in the gap on 5:1 scope
Swing free on short scope to stay small
Raft alongside the nearest boat unasked
why: Boats that cannot swing need neighbours that do not swing either.

fig.title: Late arrival, cove near Göcek
lines: Every boat lies stern-to on a shore line
One free gap in the middle

q: You anchor near a large motor yacht and a catamaran in a gusty, shifting wind. What do you allow for?
a: Extra room — they swing differently from you
o: Less room — big boats barely move
Nothing — all boats swing the same way
Their anchors hold, so yours can be lighter
why: High-windage boats sheer about more than keel yachts; leave a margin.

q: You are anchored as shown. What do you do before nightfall?
a: Re-anchor further north, out of the shoal's reach
o: Stay — the south wind keeps you north of it
Stay, and let out more chain for holding
Stay, and set the anchor alarm to warn you
why: When the wind goes north you lie south of the anchor: 35 m of chain reaches the shoal.

labels: shoal 35 m S of the anchor

q: You are motoring towards spot A to anchor. How do you make the final approach?
a: Slowly, head to wind, stopping over the spot
o: Downwind, so the wind carries you in
Across the wind at cruising speed
Fast, to keep steerage in the gusts
why: Head to wind you can stop exactly where you want and fall back in line.

q: You are head to wind over the spot. When does the bow crew let go?
a: As the boat stops and starts to drift astern
o: While still moving ahead at two knots
As soon as the spot is in sight
After drifting back a full scope
why: Letting go as you gather sternway lays the chain out instead of on the anchor.

q: The anchor is on the bottom, the boat is not moving, and the bow crew keeps running chain out fast. What happens?
a: The chain piles on the anchor and may foul it
o: The anchor digs in faster under the weight
Nothing — the scope is the same in the end
The boat is pulled forward over the anchor
why: Pay out only as fast as the boat falls back, laying the chain along the bottom.

q: You are reversing to set the anchor. What tells you it is holding?
a: Transits abeam stay fixed and the chain is taut
o: The chain goes slack and hangs straight down
The depth reading stays the same
The boat stops, then creeps slowly astern
why: A fixed transit under load proves the anchor is dug in.

q: To check the anchor is holding, which pair of objects do you line up?
a: Two fixed marks ashore, in line, abeam
o: Two yachts anchored near you, seen in line
A single headland straight ahead
A moored fishing boat and the beach behind
why: Fixed objects abeam show the smallest movement along the boat's line.

q: You set the GPS anchor alarm. Where do you centre it, and roughly what radius?
a: Centred on the anchor, about 50 m
o: Centred on the boat now, about 10 m
Centred on the anchor, about 20 m
Centred on the boat now, about 100 m
why: The antenna can be anywhere within chain plus boat length of the anchor: 34 + 12 ≈ 50 m.

fig.title: Anchor alarm
lines: Boat length 12 m, GPS at the stern

q: Your all-chain rode is set and the gusts are building. What do you rig to protect the gear?
a: A nylon snubber from a bow cleat to the chain
o: A tighter brake on the windlass gypsy
A shorter chain so it stays taut
A lashing from the chain to the pulpit
why: A snubber absorbs shock loads and takes the strain off the windlass.

q: You skipper a catamaran; the chain runs off a roller on the front beam. How do you take the load once anchored?
a: A bridle from both bow cleats to the chain
o: The chain led to one hull's bow cleat
The load left on the windlass gypsy
The chain lashed to the front beam
why: A bridle shares the load between both hulls and keeps the cat head to wind.

q: Night falls while you are at anchor in a bay. Which light do you switch on?
a: The all-round white anchor light
o: The masthead steaming light
The tricolour at the masthead
The red and green sidelights
why: Rule 30: a vessel at anchor shows an all-round white light.

q: You motor into a bay and see this yacht ahead. How do you pass it?
a: Keep clear of its bow — its chain runs out ahead
o: Close across its bow — it cannot move
Expect it to move off — the ball means leaving
As if aground — keep to deeper water
why: A black ball means at anchor; its chain runs forward from the bow.

fig.note: Yacht ahead of you in the bay

q: The water is clear and 5 m deep. What is the surest way to check the anchor has dug in?
a: Snorkel over it and look
o: Read the depth on the sounder
Wait for the anchor alarm to stay quiet
Ask the boat anchored next to you
why: In clear Med water a look at the anchor beats any guess.

q: Your plotter track looks like this. What is happening?
a: The anchor is dragging downwind
o: The boat is swinging normally on its chain
The GPS position is jumping about
The wind has shifted and you swung round
why: Swinging draws an arc; a straight line downwind means dragging.

fig.note: Your GPS track over the last hour

q: The alarm wakes you and you go on deck. What is your first action?
a: Start the engine and motor up to take the strain
o: Let out all remaining chain and wait
Call the charter base for advice
Launch the dinghy to lay a second anchor
why: The engine buys time; then lift and re-anchor or leave.

q: You decide to stay in an exposed anchorage with F7 forecast after midnight. What do you organise?
a: An anchor watch rota, engine and crew ready
o: Everyone to bed, the alarm as backup
The dinghy towed astern on a long line
Lights off to save the batteries
why: In strong wind someone stays awake, checking position, chain and neighbours.

q: You are on anchor watch when you see this. How do you respond?
a: Horn and torch to wake them; engine on, fenders out
o: Raise your anchor and leave the bay at once
Fend her off with the boathook when she arrives
Call a MAYDAY on channel 16
why: Wake the other crew and get ready to manoeuvre or fend off safely.

fig.title: 0200, wind rising
lines: A yacht upwind is dragging towards you

q: You anchored first. A yacht arrives, drops upwind and falls back to lie 5 m off your bow. What do you do?
a: Ask them politely to re-anchor further off
o: Lift your own anchor — newcomers have priority
Let out more chain to drop back from them
Say nothing and hang fenders forward
why: The first boat to anchor has priority; a newcomer must leave it room to swing.

q: Will you clear the rock when the wind goes round to the west?
a: No — the stern could reach about 52 m from the anchor
o: Yes — the rock is beyond your 40 m of chain
Yes — the boat swings only on its 40 m of chain
Yes — the curved chain keeps you within 30 m
why: Swing radius ≈ horizontal chain (about 39.5 m) + boat length 13 m ≈ 52 m > 45 m.

labels: rock is 45 m from your anchor

q: The anchor alarm goes off at 0300 in a steady F4. What do you do first?
a: Check transits, plotter track and depth
o: Silence it and go back to sleep
Start lifting the anchor straight away
Widen the alarm radius to stop it
why: Confirm whether you are really dragging before you act.

q: In a narrow anchorage you need a small swinging circle but want the bow still to turn to the wind. What do you lay?
a: A Bahamian moor: two bow anchors 180° apart
o: Bow and stern anchors, fore and aft
Two anchors in tandem on one chain
One anchor on short 2:1 scope
why: Two opposed bow anchors keep you near one spot yet let you head to wind.

q: How do you lay the two anchors?
a: Both from the bow, 30–45° apart, into the wind
o: One from the bow, one from the stern
Both on the same spot to double the weight
From the bow, 180° apart, Bahamian moor
why: A V of two bow anchors shares the load of a strong, steady wind.

fig.title: Forecast
lines: Two anchors and enough rode aboard

q: You want a quieter night without moving. What steadies the boat?
a: A stern kedge to hold her end-on to the swell
o: More chain on the bow anchor for a softer ride
A heavier nylon snubber on the bow chain
Moving in closer to the beach for shelter
why: Holding the boat end-on to the swell stops the beam-on roll.

fig.title: Anchored off Kythnos
lines: Swell rolling in from the side

q: Full astern does not move you off. What do you do next?
a: Lay the kedge by dinghy towards deep water
o: Rev hard ahead to push across the bar
Wait for the tide to fall a little further
Drop the kedge on the bar under the bow
why: A kedge laid towards deep water gives a pull the engine alone cannot.

q: You row the kedge out in the dinghy to lay it. How do you handle the rode?
a: Flake it in the dinghy and pay it out as you row
o: Leave it aboard and tow it behind the dinghy
Coil it round the anchor and throw both together
Drop the anchor first, then row the rode back
why: Paying out from the dinghy avoids dragging heavy rode through the water.

q: In a Turkish cove you take a shore line to a rock and want to leave later without going ashore. How do you rig it?
a: Round the rock and back aboard, to slip from deck
o: Made fast ashore with a bowline round the rock
Tied to the nearest bush beside the rock
Tied to your neighbour's shore line
why: A doubled line can be slipped from the boat without anyone going ashore.

q: The only shore point is a sharp-edged rock. How do you protect the line?
a: Pass a chain strop or chafe guard round the rock
o: Pull the line bar-tight so it cannot move
Use a thinner line that slides over edges
Tie it to a small bush beside the rock
why: Sharp rock saws through rope as the boat moves; protect the contact point.

q: Your stern-to berth in the cove has become uncomfortable. What do you add to fix it?
a: A second shore line on the upwind side
o: More chain out on the anchor
Extra fenders on the downwind side
A bridle rigged on the anchor chain
why: Two shore lines in a V stop the stern swinging in a cross wind.

fig.title: Cove near Göcek, stern-to the rocks
lines: Anchor out ahead, one shore line
Afternoon gusts blow across the cove

q: The anchor is down 50 m out and you have reversed to 10 m off the rocks in a light offshore breeze. What now?
a: Line ashore and back aboard, then tighten the chain
o: Tighten the chain fully, then take the line ashore
Switch off and wait for the breeze to die away
Swing on the anchor first, then take a line ashore
why: Hold position with the engine until the shore line is on; then tension against the anchor.

q: You are lifting 40 m of chain in F4. The windlass labours and the boat is not moving forward. What do you do?
a: Motor slowly up so the windlass only takes in slack
o: Keep winching — the windlass will pull the boat
Winch in short, hard bursts until it moves
Have the crew haul the chain in by hand
why: The engine moves the boat; the windlass only lifts the chain and anchor.

q: From the wheel you cannot hear the bow crew as you lift the anchor. How do they show you where the chain leads?
a: By pointing along the chain with an arm
o: By shouting louder over the wind
By banging on the deck
By calling on VHF channel 16
why: Agree hand signals before you start: point to the chain, show up-and-down, show anchor off.

q: You are lifting the anchor and reach this point. How do you break it out?
a: Lock off the chain, then motor gently ahead
o: Keep the windlass running until it frees
Drift back and pull with the windlass again
Let out 20 m more and wait an hour
why: Break an anchor out with the boat's momentum, not the windlass motor.

fig.title: Lifting the anchor
lines: Chain now straight up and down

q: The anchor is home in the bow roller and you are heading out into a lumpy sea. What do you do with it?
a: Set the chain stopper and lash the anchor down
o: Leave it held on the windlass brake alone
Lower it a metre so it cannot bang the bow
Leave the windlass breaker on, ready to drop
why: A windlass is not a stopper; a loose anchor can run out or batter the bow.

q: How do you free your anchor?
a: Hold their chain on a slip line, lower yours clear
o: Lift both and motor out dragging their chain
Motor hard ahead to jerk the anchor free of it
Ask the neighbour to cut and re-lay his chain
why: Hold the other chain on a slip line while your anchor drops free.

fig.title: Leaving a Med quay
lines: It hangs just below the surface

q: Which stern line do you let go last?
a: The windward one, rigged as a slip line
o: The leeward one, rigged as a slip line
Both at the same moment
Whichever one is easier to reach
why: The windward line stops the stern blowing onto the leeward boat until you have way on.

q: Your anchor will not break out with the chain up and down and the engine gently ahead. You have no trip line. What do you try?
a: Motor past it and pull from the other side
o: Rev ahead harder on the short chain
Let all the chain go and leave the anchor
Winch hard until the windlass frees it
why: A fouled anchor often comes out the way it went in — backwards.

q: You arrive at this town quay with a free berth. How do you moor?
a: Bow-to, so the rudder stays in deep water
o: Stern-to, but closer, so the passerelle reaches
Stern-to, with fenders over the stern
Stern-to, pushing off with a boathook
why: Bow-to keeps the rudder away from shallows at the foot of the quay.

fig.title: Pilot notes
lines: Rubble ledge just under the water
along the foot of the quay

q: You reverse into a gap on the quay. How do you keep the boat straight?
a: Get sternway early, then steer with the rudder
o: Use short bursts of full astern to stay straight
Keep the wheel hard over the whole way in
Stop and restart astern each time it swings
why: Prop walk is strongest from rest; once moving astern the rudder bites.

fig.title: Your boat astern
lines: when you first go astern from rest
No wind; gap between two yachts

q: You will moor stern-to in the marked berth. Where do you drop the anchor?
a: B — upwind of the line of the berth
o: A — straight out from the berth
C — downwind, so you drift in
Any of them — the chain straightens out
why: Dropped upwind, the chain holds the bow up to windward as you reverse.

fig.note: Wind on the beam of the berth, F4

q: You are reversing stern-to in a cross wind and the stern nears the quay. Which line goes ashore first?
a: The windward stern line
o: The leeward stern line
A bow line to the next boat
A midships spring to the quay
why: The windward line stops the stern blowing down onto the leeward neighbour.

q: You are stern-to on a town quay and conditions change as shown. How do you adjust the mooring?
a: Ease stern lines, haul in chain to sit further off
o: Tighten the stern lines to pull the boat in close
Rest the passerelle firmly down on the quay
Let out chain so the boat can move freely
why: In surge sit 1–2 m off the quay on a tight chain, with the passerelle raised.

fig.title: Town quay, swell working in
lines: Boat surging on the stern lines

q: You rig two stern lines to the bollards on the quay. How do you lead them?
a: Crossed, each quarter to the opposite bollard
o: Straight to its own bollard, left slack
Both to a single bollard in the middle
One line only, to the windward bollard
why: Crossed stern lines keep the stern centred and give longer, springier lines.

q: Reversing in, the crew is lifting the lazy line from the water at the stern. The helm wants a burst ahead to stop. What do you say?
a: Stay in neutral until the line is clear of the prop
o: Go ahead — the line is well behind the boat
Go astern instead — that is safer for the line
Steer away from the line with full rudder
why: A sinking lazy line near the stern winds easily round a turning propeller.

q: You moor bow-to on a marina pontoon with lazy lines. Where does the lazy line go?
a: Walked aft and made fast on a stern cleat
o: On the bow cleat beside the pontoon line
Led to a midships cleat
Left in the water; bow lines hold you
why: The lazy line holds the end away from the pontoon — here, the stern.

q: On a crowded town quay in Poros the harbour master tells you to reverse in straight. Why does it matter?
a: Your chain then lies clear of the neighbours' anchors
o: The passerelle then lines up with the bollards
You then need less chain to hold
Prop walk then cancels itself out
why: A chain laid at an angle crosses others and causes fouled anchors on departure.

q: What do you have ready to show?
a: Boat papers, crew list, licence, cruising tax receipt
o: Passports only — the boat is a charter boat
Nothing — papers are checked only in marinas
The insurance certificate and nothing else
why: Greek port police check boat and crew papers and the cruising tax (TEPAI).

fig.title: Town quay, Greece
lines: Port police office on the quay
An officer walks over to your boat

q: You prepare to moor stern-to between two yachts. Where do you hang the fenders?
a: Both sides, amidships and at the quarters
o: Only across the stern, facing the quay
Only on the windward side of the boat
On the bow, in case you hit the quay
why: Neighbours lie close on both sides; protect where the hulls will touch.

q: On a Greek island town quay, a long empty stretch is signed for the ferry. Can you moor there?
a: No — keep it clear for the ferry
o: Yes — an empty quay is free for all
Yes — but for one night only
Yes — if you leave before 0800
why: Ferry and tripper berths must stay clear whatever the time.

q: You pick up a buoy in a Croatian bay. It has a thin pick-up line with a loop on the end. How do you use it?
a: Only to lift the ring, then run your own line through
o: Drop its loop over a bow cleat and stay on it
Tie your line to the pick-up line
Leave it and anchor next to the buoy
why: Pick-up lines are not made for the load; never lie on one alone.

q: You are staying on a buoy for the night. How do you rig your lines to the ring?
a: From each bow cleat, through the ring, back to the same cleat
o: One line from port cleat through the ring to starboard
A single line knotted to the ring
The buoy's pick-up line on one cleat
why: Same-side loops cannot saw across the ring and can be slipped from aboard.

q: From which spot do you start your final approach to the buoy?
a: A — so you motor slowly up into the wind
o: B — so the wind carries you down onto it
C — across the wind, for a clear view
Any — at the speed the wind allows
why: Approach a buoy into the wind so you can stop beside it.

q: You lie to a buoy in a buoy field near Hvar. A boat comes by to collect a fee. What do you do?
a: Pay and keep the receipt — it is a concession
o: Refuse — buoys are free of charge in Croatia
Pay only if you stay on it after dark
Move off and anchor among the buoys
why: Croatian buoy fields are concessions; anchoring inside them is not allowed.

q: The only free buoy is a small private one with a thin chain, used by a local fishing boat. Your yacht is 14 m. Do you use it?
a: No — its ground tackle may be too light for you
o: Yes — any buoy holds a yacht in calm weather
Yes — with two lines for double strength
Yes — with longer lines to reduce snatching
why: A buoy holds only what its sinker and chain were sized for.

q: You pick up a buoy in a catamaran. How do you lie to it?
a: A line from each bow cleat to the ring, as a bridle
o: One line from the windlass roller to the ring
One line from the windward bow cleat only
The buoy pulled up tight under the front beam
why: A bridle from both hulls keeps the cat straight and stops the buoy hitting the hulls.

q: You are alongside and an offshore breeze holds the bow away from the pontoon. Which line pulls it in close?
a: A bow breast line, square to the pontoon
o: A longer bow line, led well forward
A stern spring, led forward to the pontoon
A midships spring, led aft to the pontoon
why: Breast lines run at right angles and pull the boat in; springs stop surge.

q: You are coming alongside a low floating pontoon. Where do you set the fenders?
a: Low, near the waterline, at the widest part
o: High, at the rail, to protect the deck
Only at the bow, where you touch first
Across the stern, under the passerelle
why: Fenders must sit where the hull meets the pontoon edge.

q: You come alongside this pontoon. How do you approach?
a: At a steeper angle, getting a line on fast
o: Parallel, stopped a metre off, let it blow you in
Fast and parallel, then full astern
Stern first, letting the wind hold the bow
why: Wind off the berth blows you away; aim in more and get a line ashore quickly.

q: This time the wind blows onto the berth. How do you come alongside?
a: Stop parallel, a metre off; let the wind push you in
o: At a steep angle, bow first and fairly quick
Parallel at speed, then full astern to stop
At right angles, then turn at the last moment
why: An onshore wind does the work; arrive stopped and parallel, well fendered.

q: Short-handed, you have one line on: a midships spring, led aft to a pontoon cleat. Engine gently ahead — where do you put the wheel?
a: Turned away from the pontoon, pushing the stern in
o: Turned towards the pontoon, pulling the bow in
Amidships, so the boat stays straight
Turned towards the pontoon, at full ahead
why: Against a midships spring, gentle ahead with helm away holds the boat alongside.

q: You are alongside and the wind is blowing you off the pontoon. How do you leave?
a: Let the lines go and let the wind blow you clear
o: Spring off on a bow line with full power
Push off hard from the pontoon with your feet
Motor ahead with the wheel hard towards it
why: With the wind off the berth there is no need for springs.

q: You will swing the stern out and leave astern. What do you rig, and which gear?
a: Bow spring led aft, bow fendered, gently ahead
o: Stern spring led forward, gently ahead
Bow spring led aft, gently astern
Stern line only, hard astern
why: Ahead against a bow spring pivots on the bow and swings the stern out.

q: You raft up outside a yacht of the same size on a busy town quay. What do you do?
a: Stagger the masts and run your own lines ashore
o: Line up the masts and tie only to her
Tie breast lines only, to her cleats
Borrow her shore lines to save your own
why: Staggered spreaders cannot clash; own bow and stern lines carry your load.

q: You need to cross a neighbour's yacht in a raft to get ashore late at night. How do you go?
a: Quietly across their foredeck
o: Through their cockpit — it is shortest
Knock and walk through the saloon
Along the outside of their guardrail
why: Etiquette: cross by the foredeck, keep clear of the cockpit.

q: How do you set your lines?
a: Long springs, slack left in bow and stern lines
o: Short lines, all bar-tight to hold you close
Breast lines only, made up tight
Tight now, adjusted in the morning
why: Long lines tolerate a change of level; tight short ones hang the boat.

q: How do you protect the hull?
a: A fender board outside the fenders
o: Fenders hung flat between the piles
Fewer fenders, so they cannot roll off
Fenders tied to the piles themselves
why: A plank outside the fenders spans the piles so the fenders cannot slip between.

q: You are coming alongside a pontoon with room on either side. Which side do you put to it, and why?
a: Port side-to — the stop astern pulls the stern in
o: Starboard side-to — astern pulls the stern in
Port side-to — astern pushes the stern clear
Either — prop walk acts only in ahead
why: Use prop walk: the burst astern to stop walks the stern towards the berth.

q: You check the anchor locker before the season. How should the bitter end of the chain be secured?
a: With a strong lashing that can be cut
o: Shackled tight so it can never be lost
Loose in the locker, ready to run
Wound twice round the windlass drum
why: If the anchor must be abandoned, the chain can be cut free in seconds.

q: You have lifted the anchor and are motoring out of the bay. What do you do with this?
a: Lower it — it says you are at anchor
o: Keep it up until clear of the bay
Keep it up while motoring
Leave it up until you hoist sail
why: The ball means at anchor; take it down as soon as you are under way.
